turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, grab a seat. You look a bit wound up, so just start wherever you like.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, um, I've got this rash and it's so itchy I can't think straight. I don't know if it was something I ate or the new cream or the antibiotic, and I keep going round in circles.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We've been up half the night with it. I thought we should get it looked at rather than wait the weekend out.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not just a bit of itch, it's, like, burning itchy. Sorry, I'm talking too fast, aren't I.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're right to come in. Whereabouts is the rash, and how long's it been there?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Arms and my stomach. It started three days ago. I remember because I had that work thing on Wednesday and I was fine then.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was longer than that. You were scratching last Monday, so that's a week. I saw the marks on your forearm when I was doing the washing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Monday? No. I would've said something. It's three days, I'm sure. Well, pretty sure.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, so we're somewhere between about three days and a week, and we won't pretend we've nailed the start. Is the itch there all the time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much constant, worse at night. I haven't slept properly the last two nights, I just lie there scratching. Does that mean it's getting into my blood or something?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not from itch alone, no. Any swelling of the lips or tongue, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Breathing's been normal. But could it still suddenly close my throat? That's what I keep picturing.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): If there's been no swelling and you're breathing fine sitting here, a sudden collapse is unlikely, but we'll go through what to watch for before you leave. Tell me about the food first.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Prawns. At my brother's barbie. I had a pile of them. Then this. Or it might've already been starting, I can't line it up in my head.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the cream. You opened that new tube the same week, the DermaVeen one from the chemist, for dry skin.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, DermaVeen. I put it on my arms two nights, maybe three. Can a moisturiser even do this? It says it's for sensitive skin.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can, in some people, even the gentle ones. A contact irritation or an allergy to something in the cream is on the list. And the antibiotic?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin, for the sinus infection. Tablets. I think it's five hundred milligrams, twice a day. The GP started it, um, five days ago.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not what the bottle says. It's two hundred and fifty milligrams, three times a day. I've been putting them in the dosette, so I'm looking at it every morning.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Two fifty? I swear he said five hundred. God, have I been taking the wrong amount? Is that why I've got the rash?

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Easy. I don't want to guess a dose when you're each remembering a different one. Bring the box next time, or the carer can read it to us later. Five days on it, you both happy with that bit?
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Friday just gone, yes, five days. That part's right.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I even take the next one? And, look, she keeps bringing up penicillin. I'm not allergic to penicillin. I've had it before.

[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm not making it up. Your sister told me when I moved in, and it's written in the old health summary in the folder: rash with penicillin as a child. This looks the same to me.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): That summary is wrong. I told the last doctor to take it off. I don't remember any rash as a kid, and I'm not allergic. Why is that still in there?

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm hearing two different stories and I'm not going to stamp penicillin allergy on you today, or wipe it either. We'll just keep it in mind. Let me have a look at the skin.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it going to scar? Is it infected? It feels hot.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forearms and across the tummy there's a red blotchy rash, flat, no blisters, skin isn't broken. Lips aren't swollen. It looks irritated, not an infection I can see.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Okay. So not infected. What about my temperature and all that, is that normal? I feel a bit flushed but that might just be panic.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temp's thirty-six point nine, pulse is eighty-two, oxygen's ninety-seven percent, and blood pressure's one-eighteen over seventy-four. All very ordinary.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): See, I told you in the car you weren't about to keel over. Speaking of the car, that freeway was a nightmare, wasn't it.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh don't start me on the freeway. We sat at that roadworks for, I don't know, forty minutes. Some bloke in a ute was playing the cricket so loud I could hear it with the windows up.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was the one-dayer. I only caught the tail end at home. Bowling was all over the place, then they dragged it back.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I had the radio on while I was making a cuppa yesterday and I still don't know who won. The dog hated the commentary, kept barking at the speaker.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): What sort of dog?
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Little fox terrier, Biscuit. Mad as a cut snake when the postie comes, otherwise just sleeps on the good couch, which she's not allowed to do.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): She did that thing again where she steals the socks and lines them up in the hallway. I nearly tripped. And the weather, it's been so sticky I don't even want to walk her.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sticky is right. I had the fan on and it just pushed hot air around. Supposed to cool down after Thursday, if you believe the forecast.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forecasts have been hopeless this month. Right. Back to this rash, before we lose the thread.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. Yeah. So what do you actually think it is? I need a name for it or I'll keep googling and scaring myself.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't give you a firm one. It could be the prawns, it could be something in the DermaVeen, or it could be the amoxicillin, and I can't separate those from what I can see today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So all three are still possible? Am I contagious? Can I go to work tomorrow, I sit next to people?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not contagious, no. Work's fine if you feel up to it and you're not drowsy from anything we start. I'd like you to start an antihistamine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Which one? Will it knock me out? I have to drive the carer to the shops some arvos. And what if it doesn't work?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cetirizine, ten milligrams, once a day, take it at night. It can make some people a bit sleepy, so see how you go before you drive. If the itch is still miserable we can rethink, but let's start there.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll pick that up from the chemist on the way home. What do we do with the cream and the prawns, and those tablets?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the DermaVeen for now, and give prawns a miss until this has settled. I'd hold the amoxicillin too, don't take the next doses, and we'll let your GP know there was a rash. The sinus infection itself I haven't rechecked today.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Hold it completely? What if the sinus comes roaring back? And the patch test thing, someone at work said rashes need a patch test. Do I need that? Does it hurt?

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the rash hasn't settled in a couple of weeks we might arrange patch testing, to see whether a chemical in a cream is involved. It shouldn't hurt, little discs on the skin, read a few days later. I'm not booking it now.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of weeks is a long time to be this itchy. What if I wake up and my tongue's fat? Do I call you, or an ambulance, or what?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): If your lips or tongue swell, or you can't breathe properly, or you feel faint, that's an ambulance, don't wait for me. Otherwise, if it's not better in a week, come back and we'll look again.

[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll keep an eye overnight and we've got the after-hours number on the fridge. I'll bring the amoxicillin box to the GP as well so someone can read the actual strength.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'd help a lot. You've done the right thing coming in. Try not to scratch it raw, cool cloth if you need, and we'll take it from there.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
